title: Bloom filters: a tiny 'maybe' that saves a trip to disk
dek: In 1970 Burton Bloom asked how much memory you can save if a membership test may sometimes say yes when the answer is no. His answer, a row of bits and a few hash functions, now sits in front of almost every database file, web crawler and cache.

items: A Bloom filter answers 'is this in the set?' with either 'definitely not' or 'probably yes', using a fraction of the memory the set itself needs.
It is an array of bits and k hash functions. Adding an item sets k bits; checking an item looks at the same k bits; any 0 means it was never added.
About 10 bits per item gives under 1% false positives. You can't remove items or list them, and a 'yes' still has to be checked against the real data.

body.x: The paper: "Space/Time Trade-offs in Hash Coding with Allowable Errors" by Burton H. Bloom, Communications of the ACM, July 1970.

Bloom's example was a hyphenation program. Of 500,000 English words, about 450,000 could be hyphenated by simple rules; the other 50,000 needed a dictionary on disk, which was slow. The program needed to know, for each word, whether it was one of the hard ones. Keeping the 50,000 words in memory was too expensive in 1970. But a test that was sometimes wrong in one direction, saying 'hard' for an easy word, only cost an occasional unnecessary disk read, while never missing a hard one.

body.cap: Each item sets the same k bits every time, so if any of an item's bits is 0, it was never added. When all its bits are 1 it was probably added, but other items may have set those bits: that is a false positive, and it is the only kind of mistake a Bloom filter makes.

items: Start with m bits, all 0, and choose k independent hash functions.
To add an item, compute its k hashes and set those k bits to 1.
To check an item, look at its k bits. Any 0: definitely not in the set. All 1: probably in it.
False negatives are impossible; false positives are bounded and tunable.

body.cap: The error rate depends only on bits per item and the number of hash functions. With the best number of hashes, about 0.7 × bits per item, every 2 extra bits per item cut false positives by more than half.

body.x: Compare that with storing the items: a crawler's 1 crore URLs at about 100 bytes each take a gigabyte, while a Bloom filter that is right 99% of the time takes about 12 MB.

items: Remove an item: clearing its bits could clear bits other items need. A counting Bloom filter, with a small counter per position instead of a bit, can delete at the cost of more memory.
List what is in the set, or count it exactly.
Say 'yes' for certain: a 'probably' must be confirmed against the real data when a wrong yes matters.
Stay accurate if it fills beyond the number of items it was sized for: false positives climb fast.
In front of every SSTable in Bigtable, Cassandra and RocksDB, so a read skips files that can't hold the key (see the Bigtable paper).
In web crawlers, to skip URLs already fetched without keeping every URL in memory (the Web crawler problem).
In CDNs and caches, to store an object only on its second request, so one-off requests don't push out popular files.
In apps that must not show the same item twice, such as profiles already swiped (the Dating swipes problem).
Reach for a Bloom filter when you need 'have I seen this?' over a huge set, memory is tight, and an occasional false 'yes' is cheap to double-check.
Size it out loud: items × 10 bits for about 1% error.
Say what a false positive costs in your design: an extra database read is fine; refusing a username that is actually free may not be, so confirm 'yes' answers against the database.
Mention that it can't delete, and what you'd do instead: rebuild it periodically, or use a counting filter.

body.x: With m bits, n items and k hash functions, the chance a given bit is still 0 after all insertions is about e^(−kn/m), so the false-positive rate is about (1 − e^(−kn/m))^k. It is smallest when k = (m/n) × ln 2, about 0.69 × bits per item, and then the rate is about 0.6185^(m/n). That last number is why each extra bit per item cuts the error to about 62% of what it was.
